outputs.L4:
Since the 1970s, mainland Britain has experienced repeated bombing campaigns and attempted attacks by terrorist organizations, state-linked operatives, extremist networks, and self-radicalized individuals. Their targets have included government buildings, military personnel, public transportation, airports, businesses, entertainment venues, and crowded public spaces. The chronology of these incidents reveals both the changing nature of terrorism in the United Kingdom and the growing importance of intelligence, forensic investigation, emergency planning, and preventive policing.

During the 1970s and 1980s, many of the most serious bombings were connected to the conflict in Northern Ireland. The Provisional Irish Republican Army carried out attacks intended to cause casualties, economic disruption, and political pressure. In 1974, bombs at two pubs in Birmingham killed 21 people, while attacks in Guildford and Woolwich killed seven more. Later incidents included the 1983 Harrods bombing in London, in which six people died, and the 1984 bombing of the Grand Hotel in Brighton during the Conservative Party conference. The Brighton attack, an attempt to assassinate Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and members of her government, killed five people. These cases led to extensive police investigations, although some also produced serious miscarriages of justice, including the wrongful convictions of the Birmingham Six and Guildford Four.

The period also saw terrorism from other sources. The left-wing Angry Brigade carried out a series of comparatively small bomb attacks in the early 1970s, generally targeting political, military, and commercial property. In December 1988, Pan Am Flight 103 was destroyed by a bomb over Lockerbie in Scotland, killing all 259 people on the aircraft and 11 people on the ground. The investigation became one of the largest and most complex in British history and eventually resulted in the conviction of a Libyan intelligence officer.

The IRA continued to attack mainland economic and political targets in the 1990s. A bomb at the Baltic Exchange in the City of London in 1992 killed three people and caused extensive damage. The 1993 Bishopsgate bombing killed one person and devastated another part of London’s financial district. In 1996, a bomb at South Quay in London’s Docklands killed two people, while a much larger device detonated in central Manchester later that year. Police evacuated tens of thousands of people after receiving a warning, and although more than 200 were injured, no one was killed. The Manchester evacuation demonstrated how rapid police action could greatly reduce casualties even when an explosion could not be prevented.

In April 1999, far-right extremist David Copeland planted three nail bombs in London. The devices targeted Black residents in Brixton, the Bangladeshi community in Brick Lane, and the LGBT community in Soho. The Soho bombing killed three people, including a pregnant woman, and the three attacks injured more than 100. CCTV images, witness information, and coordinated police work helped investigators identify and arrest Copeland within days.

In the twenty-first century, the principal threat increasingly came from violent Islamist extremism. On 7 July 2005, four suicide bombers attacked three London Underground trains and a bus. They killed 52 victims and injured hundreds in the deadliest terrorist attack in Britain since Lockerbie. Two weeks later, another group attempted to repeat the attacks, but their devices failed to explode properly. The suspects fled, prompting a large-scale manhunt and a series of arrests. The failed 21 July attacks illustrated both the continuing danger and the value of CCTV, forensic evidence, public assistance, and international police cooperation.

Several major plots were disrupted before they could be carried out. In 2004, police and the security services broke up a conspiracy involving large quantities of ammonium nitrate fertilizer that could have been used against targets such as shopping centres or public utilities. In 2006, investigators uncovered a plan to use liquid explosives against transatlantic passenger aircraft departing from Britain. The arrests prevented a potentially catastrophic attack and led to major changes in airport security, including restrictions on liquids in hand luggage.

Not every attempted attack was stopped in advance. In 2007, two car bombs containing fuel and gas cylinders were discovered in central London before they detonated. The following day, members of the same network drove a burning vehicle into the terminal at Glasgow Airport. No members of the public were killed, although one attacker later died from his injuries. In September 2017, an improvised device partially exploded on a London Underground train at Parsons Green, injuring dozens but failing to produce the mass casualties apparently intended.

The 2017 Manchester Arena bombing was far more destructive. A suicide attacker detonated a device as people were leaving a concert, killing 22 victims and injuring many others. The attack led to an extensive investigation into the bomber’s contacts and preparation, as well as public inquiries examining venue security and the emergency response. Other incidents, including the 2021 bombing outside Liverpool Women’s Hospital, showed that individuals could still assemble explosive devices with limited assistance. In the Liverpool case, the device detonated inside a taxi, killing the bomber; the driver survived.

Taken together, these attacks demonstrate that terrorism in mainland Britain has not come from a single movement or ideology. Irish republican groups, far-right extremists, violent Islamists, state-linked actors, and isolated individuals have all used or attempted to use explosives. Their methods have ranged from timed car bombs and concealed devices to suicide attacks and improvised explosives made from commercially available materials.

The chronology also shows that terrorist plans do not always succeed. Some devices have malfunctioned, while others have been found and made safe after alert members of the public reported suspicious vehicles or packages. Intelligence operations, surveillance, border controls, forensic science, CCTV, emergency evacuations, and cooperation between police and security agencies have disrupted several potentially devastating conspiracies. Although such measures cannot eliminate every threat, effective policing and counterterrorism work have repeatedly prevented attacks, limited casualties, and enabled those responsible to be identified and prosecuted.

counterfactuals.output:
## Major bombings and attempted bomb attacks in mainland Britain, 1970s–June 2007

*Selective chronology; Northern Ireland attacks are excluded. Fatality figures generally exclude perpetrators unless noted.*

### 1970s

- **March 8, 1973 — London:** An IRA car bomb explodes outside the Old Bailey courthouse, killing one person and injuring about 200. A second device near Whitehall is defused.
- **February 4, 1974 — Yorkshire:** An IRA bomb aboard a coach on the M62 kills 12 people, including soldiers and members of their families.
- **June 17, 1974 — London:** An IRA bomb explodes at the Houses of Parliament, injuring 11.
- **July 17, 1974 — London:** A bomb at the Tower of London kills one person and injures more than 40.
- **October 5, 1974 — Guildford:** IRA bombs at two pubs used by soldiers kill five people and injure dozens.
- **November 7, 1974 — Woolwich, London:** An IRA bomb at the Kings Arms pub kills two and injures more than 30.
- **November 21, 1974 — Birmingham:** Bombs destroy two crowded pubs, killing 21 people and injuring more than 180—the deadliest terrorist attack in mainland Britain until 2005.
- **September 5, 1975 — London:** An IRA bomb at the Hilton hotel kills two people and injures more than 60.
- **November–December 1975 — London:** An IRA unit carries out bombings and shootings before being trapped in the six-day **Balcombe Street siege**.

### 1980s

- **July 20, 1982 — London:** Coordinated IRA bombs strike military ceremonies in Hyde Park and Regent’s Park, killing 11 soldiers and seven horses.
- **December 17, 1983 — London:** An IRA car bomb outside Harrods department store kills six people, including three police officers, and injures about 90.
- **October 12, 1984 — Brighton:** An IRA bomb tears through the Grand Hotel during the Conservative Party conference. Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher escapes; five people are killed.
- **December 21, 1988 — Lockerbie, Scotland:** A bomb destroys Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, killing all 259 aboard and 11 people on the ground.
- **September 22, 1989 — Deal, Kent:** An IRA bomb at the Royal Marines School of Music kills 11 military bandsmen and injures more than 20.

### 1990s

- **February 7, 1991 — London:** The IRA fires three homemade mortar shells at 10 Downing Street while Prime Minister John Major and his Cabinet are meeting. No one is killed.
- **April 10, 1992 — London:** An IRA truck bomb at the Baltic Exchange kills three people, injures more than 90 and causes extensive damage to the financial district.
- **March 20, 1993 — Warrington:** Two IRA bombs placed in litter bins kill two boys, aged 3 and 12, and injure dozens.
- **April 24, 1993 — London:** A massive IRA truck bomb in Bishopsgate kills one person, injures more than 40 and devastates part of the City of London.
- **February 9, 1996 — London:** An IRA truck bomb at South Quay in the Docklands ends a 17-month ceasefire, killing two people and injuring more than 100.
- **June 15, 1996 — Manchester:** An IRA truck bomb explodes in the city center after warnings and evacuation. No one is killed, but more than 200 are injured and large sections of the commercial district are destroyed.
- **April 17–30, 1999 — London:** Neo-Nazi David Copeland carries out nail-bomb attacks in Brixton, Brick Lane and Soho. The Soho bombing kills three people, including a pregnant woman, and the series injures more than 100.

### 2000–2004

- **March 4, 2001 — London:** A Real IRA car bomb explodes outside BBC Television Centre. One person suffers minor injuries.
- **August 3, 2001 — Ealing, London:** A Real IRA car bomb injures seven people and damages shops and homes.
- **November 3, 2001 — Birmingham:** A Real IRA car bomb fails to detonate fully in the city center; police had cleared the area after a warning.

### 2005

- **July 7 — London:** Four Islamist suicide bombers strike three Underground trains and a bus during the morning rush hour. Fifty-two victims are killed and more than 700 injured.
- **July 21 — London:** Four attempted bombings target three Underground trains and a bus. The detonators fire but the main explosive charges fail; no one is killed. The suspects flee and are later captured.

### 2007

- **June 29 — London:** Police discover two Mercedes cars packed with fuel, gas cylinders and nails—one near the Tiger Tiger nightclub in Haymarket and another linked vehicle later found in Park Lane. Both devices fail to explode.
- **June 30 — Glasgow:** Two men drive a Jeep Cherokee loaded with fuel and gas cylinders into the terminal entrance at Glasgow Airport. The vehicle catches fire but does not explode as intended. Several people are injured; one attacker later dies from burns.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the history of bombings and foiled bombing plots in England, Scotland, and Wales between February 1974 and June 2007, formatted as a dated news chronology.
counterfactuals.output:
## Bombings and foiled bombing plots in Britain, February 1974–June 2007

*The chronology covers the principal fatal, mass-casualty, politically significant, and major foiled attacks in England, Scotland, and Wales. It does not include every hoax, incendiary attack, or small unexploded device.*

### 1974

- **4 February 1974 — M62, West Yorkshire, England:** An IRA bomb hidden aboard a coach carrying service personnel and their families exploded near Batley. Twelve people were killed, including two children, and more than 30 injured.

- **17 June 1974 — Westminster, London:** An IRA bomb exploded at the Houses of Parliament, injuring 11 and causing extensive damage.

- **17 July 1974 — Tower of London:** A bomb exploded in the White Tower, killing one visitor and injuring more than 40. The attack was generally attributed to the IRA.

- **5 October 1974 — Guildford, Surrey:** IRA bombs struck two pubs used by soldiers, killing five people and injuring about 65. The Guildford Four were wrongly convicted; their convictions were quashed in 1989.

- **7 November 1974 — Woolwich, London:** A bomb at the Kings Arms pub killed a soldier and a civilian and injured more than 30.

- **21 November 1974 — Birmingham:** Bombs exploded in the Mulberry Bush and Tavern in the Town pubs, killing 21 and injuring more than 180—the deadliest terrorist attack in England in the 20th century. The Birmingham Six were wrongly convicted and cleared in 1991.

### 1975–1976

- **27 January 1975 — Manchester:** An IRA bomb at Lewis’s department store injured around 20 people.

- **28 August 1975 — Caterham, Surrey:** An IRA bomb in a pub frequented by soldiers injured more than 30.

- **5 September 1975 — London Hilton:** An IRA bomb killed two people and injured more than 60.

- **9 October 1975 — Green Park, London:** A bomb at a bus stop killed one person and injured about 20.

- **12 November 1975 — Mayfair, London:** An IRA bomb thrown into Scott’s restaurant killed one person and injured 15.

- **6–12 December 1975 — Balcombe Street, London:** Four IRA gunmen took hostages after being pursued by police. Their surrender ended a prolonged bombing campaign and helped investigators connect the cell to several London attacks.

- **4 March 1976 — Cannon Street, London:** A bomb exploded on an Underground train. The attacker was killed and several passengers were injured.

### 1979–1984

- **30 March 1979 — Westminster, London:** Irish National Liberation Army members killed Conservative MP Airey Neave with a bomb placed under his car as he left the Palace of Westminster.

- **10 October 1981 — Chelsea Barracks, London:** An IRA bomb killed two civilians and injured about 40.

- **26 October 1981 — Oxford Street, London:** Metropolitan Police explosives officer Kenneth Howorth was killed while attempting to defuse an IRA bomb in a Wimpy restaurant.

- **20 July 1982 — Hyde Park and Regent’s Park, London:** Coordinated IRA attacks targeted military ceremonies. A car bomb in Hyde Park killed four Household Cavalry soldiers and seven horses; a bomb beneath the Regent’s Park bandstand killed seven Royal Green Jackets bandsmen. Scores were injured.

- **17 December 1983 — Harrods, London:** An IRA car bomb killed six people—three police officers and three civilians—and injured about 90.

- **12 October 1984 — Brighton, England:** An IRA time bomb devastated the Grand Hotel during the Conservative Party conference. Five people were killed and more than 30 injured. Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher escaped.

### 1988–1991

- **21 December 1988 — Lockerbie, Scotland:** A bomb destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, killing all 259 people aboard and 11 residents on the ground. Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted in 2001, although the case remained controversial. It was the deadliest terrorist bombing in British history.

- **22 September 1989 — Deal, Kent:** An IRA bomb destroyed part of the Royal Marines School of Music, killing 11 bandsmen and injuring more than 20.

- **20 July 1990 — City of London:** The IRA bombed the London Stock Exchange. No one was killed because warnings allowed evacuation, but the building suffered major damage.

- **7 February 1991 — Downing Street, London:** The IRA fired three improvised mortar shells at No. 10 while Prime Minister John Major and the War Cabinet were meeting. The shells missed the building; no one was killed.

- **18 February 1991 — Victoria and Paddington stations, London:** IRA bombs struck the rail network. The Victoria explosion killed one person and injured nearly 40; the Paddington device caused no casualties.

### 1992–1994

- **10 April 1992 — Baltic Exchange, City of London:** A large IRA truck bomb killed three people, injured more than 90, and caused massive financial damage.

- **12 October 1992 — Covent Garden, London:** A bomb in the Sussex Arms pub killed one person and injured several others.

- **26 February 1993 — Warrington, Cheshire:** IRA bombs damaged gas-storage facilities. A police officer was shot and wounded as the bombers escaped.

- **20 March 1993 — Warrington:** Two bombs placed in litter bins exploded in a busy shopping district, killing three-year-old Johnathan Ball and 12-year-old Tim Parry and injuring more than 50.

- **24 April 1993 — Bishopsgate, City of London:** An enormous IRA truck bomb killed a newspaper photographer, injured more than 40, and caused damage estimated at hundreds of millions of pounds.

- **9, 11 and 13 March 1994 — Heathrow Airport, London:** The IRA fired improvised mortar bombs at the airport on three occasions. None detonated, but the attacks exposed serious security vulnerabilities and repeatedly disrupted flights.

### 1996–1997

- **9 February 1996 — Docklands, London:** The IRA ended its 17-month ceasefire with a truck bomb at South Quay near Canary Wharf. Two people were killed, more than 100 injured, and surrounding buildings heavily damaged.

- **15 June 1996 — Manchester:** An IRA truck bomb exploded in the city centre after a warning and mass evacuation. More than 200 people were injured; no one was killed. It was one of the largest bombs detonated in Britain since the Second World War.

- **5 April 1997 — Aintree, Merseyside:** Bomb warnings forced the evacuation and postponement of the Grand National. No bomb was found, but about 60,000 spectators were stranded overnight.

- **1997 — English transport network:** IRA bomb warnings and several devices caused extensive rail and motorway disruption before the organization restored its ceasefire in July.

### 1999

- **17 April 1999 — Brixton, London:** A nail bomb planted by neo-Nazi David Copeland injured dozens in an area with a large Black population.

- **24 April 1999 — Brick Lane, London:** Copeland’s second nail bomb targeted the Bangladeshi community and injured several people.

- **30 April 1999 — Soho, London:** Copeland’s third bomb exploded in the Admiral Duncan, a gay pub. Three people were killed and scores injured. Copeland was later convicted of murder.

### 2000–2001

- **20 September 2000 — MI6 headquarters, London:** The Real IRA fired an anti-tank rocket at the intelligence service’s building at Vauxhall Cross. The rocket caused damage but no casualties.

- **4 March 2001 — BBC Television Centre, London:** A Real IRA car bomb exploded outside the BBC in White City, injuring one person and damaging the entrance.

- **3 August 2001 — Ealing, London:** A Real IRA car bomb injured seven people and damaged shops and homes.

- **3 November 2001 — Birmingham:** A Real IRA car bomb was discovered in the city centre. Police evacuated the area; the device exploded without causing casualties.

### 2004: major Islamist plots disrupted

- **30 March 2004 — Operation Crevice, England:** Police arrested members of a British Islamist cell and seized about 600 kilograms of ammonium-nitrate fertilizer stored in west London. The group had discussed bombing targets including shopping, entertainment, and utility sites. Five men were convicted in 2007.

- **August 2004 — London:** Dhiren Barot was arrested after surveillance revealed plans for coordinated attacks, including a radioactive “dirty bomb,” explosive-packed limousines, and attacks on financial buildings. No functioning bomb had yet been assembled. Barot pleaded guilty in 2006 to conspiracy to murder.

### 2005

- **7 July 2005 — London:** Four suicide bombers attacked three Underground trains and a bus. Fifty-two victims were killed and more than 700 injured. It was Britain’s first successful Islamist suicide-bombing operation.

- **21 July 2005 — London:** Four attempted suicide bombs were planted on three Underground trains and a bus. Their main charges failed to detonate, causing only minor injuries. The bombers fled but were subsequently captured and convicted.

### 2006

- **10 August 2006 — Transatlantic aircraft plot foiled:** British authorities arrested suspects accused of planning to smuggle liquid explosives aboard passenger aircraft departing Heathrow for North America and detonate them in flight. The operation led to sweeping restrictions on liquids in hand luggage. Several conspirators were later convicted.

### 2007

- **29 June 2007 — Central London:** Police discovered two Mercedes cars packed with petrol, gas cylinders, and nails—one outside the Tiger Tiger nightclub and another nearby after it had been towed. Neither device detonated. Investigators linked the plot to the following day’s attack in Scotland.

- **30 June 2007 — Glasgow Airport, Scotland:** Two men drove a Jeep containing petrol and gas cylinders into the terminal and set it alight. Several people were injured; attacker Kafeel Ahmed later died from burns. The incident was treated as an Islamist terrorist attack connected to the failed London car bombs.

### Geographic perspective

- **England** experienced nearly all the IRA’s major mainland bombing campaigns and all the successful or attempted Islamist attacks before July 2007.
- **Scotland’s** defining event was the 1988 Lockerbie bombing, followed by the Glasgow Airport attack in June 2007.
- **Wales** experienced threats, minor explosive incidents, and politically motivated arson during the period—particularly Welsh-nationalist attacks on holiday homes—but no bombing on the mass-casualty scale seen in England or at Lockerbie. Many Welsh nationalist incidents involved incendiaries rather than conventional bombs and are therefore normally treated separately from this bombing chronology.
